problems.location: Concept 2: Memory Reconstruction, Schema Formation, and Knowledge Integration / block 1
problems.lesson_text: ### The Fallacy of the Mental File Cabinet
problems.source_text: Focus primarily on the slides, with the other two sources being additional information to fill in any gaps or as “fun facts”.
problems.reason: Concepts 2, 3, 4, 6 and most of 7 (memory, motivation, study strategies, multimedia design, aging brains) come from How People Learn II, so the lesson is built mainly on a supporting source rather than the slides.

problems.location: Exercise 1.1: Differentiating surface vs structural variations in workforce learning ecologies using contrasting cases / block 1
problems.lesson_text: A new nurse joins a hospital ward and, during her first week, spends most of her time observing experienced nurses as they conduct patient rounds
problems.source_text: This is for an educational audience, so make sure all exercises have relevant examples to education leaders, such as L&D leaders or district leaders in schools.
problems.reason: Most exercises use nurses, programmers, medical students and graduate students rather than cases an L&D leader or district leader would face.

problems.location: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
problems.lesson_text: Examine the dynamic interaction of sociocultural contexts, cognitive processes, and motivational factors in shaping memory reconstruction and knowledge integration.
problems.source_text: Appraise claims and evidence about AI and learning, including when the evidence does not yet exist / Design AI-enabled learning experiences in which developmental consequences shaped what got built / This lesson primarily focuses on the first 3 of these objectives.
problems.reason: The lesson's objectives drop the requested focus on appraising AI evidence, designing AI-enabled learning and judging capacity-building by age and stage, and replace it with memory and motivation science.

problems.location: Exercise 1.2: Mapping professional development pathways across the six touchpoints of situated learning ecologies / block 1
problems.lesson_text: the six primary touchpoints of learning ecologies: formal instruction, informal learning, mentorship, peer collaboration, community engagement, and work-based practices
problems.source_text: Six places people learn at work / Required formal / Self-paced / Outside learning / Community-based / Relational / Work-based
problems.reason: This list of six touchpoints differs from the source's six places (it drops self-paced and outside learning and splits relational and community-based differently), and it contradicts the lesson's own Concept 1 cards.

problems.location: Concept 4: Evidence-Based Cognitive Learning Strategies and Self-Regulation / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Juxtaposing contrasting problem sets forces the brain to identify deep structural attributes rather than superficial surface markers, tripling the capacity to transfer concepts to novel scenarios.
problems.source_text: Twelfth-grade students who completed the module nearly tripled their abilities to translate between graphs and equations, even though they had previously completed algebra.
problems.reason: In the source the near-tripling is one perceptual-learning module's gain in translating graphs and equations, not a general effect of interleaving on transfer to new situations; the source also notes that blocked practice sometimes helps.

problems.location: Concept 7: Lifelong Learning, Workforce Training Transfer, and Adaptive Development / block 1
problems.lesson_text: A robust **transfer climate** relies on three systemic levers: ... **3. Psychological Safety and Error Tolerance**
problems.source_text: The authors point to three elements in the work environment that are important: 1. Environmental support for training, including peer and supervisor support 2. Transfer climate, in the form of implicit cues in the environment that using what is learned in training on the job is expected ... 3. Organizational constraints, such as lack of autonomy and other situational factors
problems.reason: The source's three work-environment elements are environmental support, transfer climate and organizational constraints; the lesson makes transfer climate the umbrella and swaps organizational constraints for psychological safety.

problems.location: Concept 2: Memory Reconstruction, Schema Formation, and Knowledge Integration / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Synthetic misconception: students invent edge boundaries to prevent falling off
problems.source_text: Many children said that the Earth is round but also stated that it has an end or edge from which people could fall.
problems.reason: In the source the edge is where people could fall off, and people stay safe by living on top of the pancake; the lesson reverses this, saying the edges prevent falling.

problems.location: Exercise 7.1: Designing organizational policies that foster supportive transfer climates for near and far training transfer / block 2
problems.lesson_text: If an older worker compensates for slower processing speed by using checklists and reminders, what kind of mechanism is this? ... Neurocognitive compensatory mechanism
problems.source_text: Older adults often recruit regions bilaterally (from both left and right cerebral hemispheres) ... Technologies may support cognition and learning in older adults by providing cognitive aids
problems.reason: The source uses compensation in the brain to mean recruiting extra brain regions, and calls checklists and reminders cognitive aids, so the answer key's label is wrong.

problems.location: Exercise 5.1: Auditing institutional software to unpack invisible algorithmic processes across choosing, judging, and sorting functions / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Learner outcomes are maximized when visible and invisible AI systems are intentionally combined, as this dual approach enhances agency, metacognitive cues, and ethical decision-making in educational environments.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. ... There’s no one right relationship with this stuff. Start with the learner in front of you.
problems.reason: The exercise has students accept a made-up general conclusion that combining AI types maximizes outcomes, while the source says no form of AI is good or bad on its own and there is no one right approach.

problems.location: Concept 7: Lifelong Learning, Workforce Training Transfer, and Adaptive Development / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Interventions that automate away entry-level cognitive tasks prevent emerging professionals from building the tacit mental models and pattern recognition required for long-term expertise.
problems.source_text: How do emerging workers build expertise and a foundation for pattern recognition when the foundational work that builds it is disappearing?
problems.reason: The source asks this as an open question, but the lesson states it as a settled finding.
